items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A situation in which some factors of production are idle, so the economy produces inside its PPC"?
items.answer: unemployment of resources
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of unemployment of resources.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a movement from inside to onto the PPC and a movement along the PPC.
items.answer: A movement along the curve reallocates fully employed resources, so one good is sacrificed for the other; moving from inside to the curve uses previously unemployed resources, so output of both goods can rise with no opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: A movement along the curve reallocates fully employed resources, so one good is sacrificed for the other; moving from inside to the curve uses previously unemployed resources, so output of both goods can rise with no opportunity cost. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mei writes: "A point inside the PPC is unattainable." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A point inside the PPC is attainable but inefficient (resources are unemployed or wasted); points outside the curve are unattainable.
items.markingKey: A point inside the PPC is attainable but inefficient (resources are unemployed or wasted); points outside the curve are unattainable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the shift of US factories to military production during the Second World War, explain how it illustrates opportunity cost shown by a PPC.
items.answer: Car plants such as Ford's were converted to build tanks and aircraft, and civilian car production almost stopped. The economy moved along its PPC towards military goods; the opportunity cost was the civilian goods no longer produced.
items.markingKey: Context (Car plants such as Ford's were converted to build tanks and aircraft, and civilian car production almost stopped.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The economy moved along its PPC towards military goods; the opportunity cost was the civilian goods no longer produced. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to opportunity cost shown by a PPC.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate why a production possibilities curve is concave to the origin and how it illustrates increasing opportunity cost, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: good X on the horizontal axis, good Y on the vertical axis; a concave PPC. Moving from A to B to C, each equal increase in X requires a larger fall in Y, because resources best suited to Y are increasingly used for X. Points on the curve are productively efficient; inside: unemployment; outside: unattainable.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: good X on the horizontal axis, good Y on the vertical axis; a concave PPC. Moving from A to B to C, each equal increase in X requires a larger fall in Y, because resources best suited to Y are increasingly used for X. Points on the curve are productively efficient; inside: unemployment; outside: unattainable. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: The table shows the production possibilities of Ruritania producing fish (tonnes) (first number) and timber (m³) (second number): (0, 73), (5, 65), (10, 51), (15, 29), (20, 0). Calculate the opportunity cost per unit of fish when output rises from 15 to 20, and from 10 to 15. Explain what your results show about the shape of the PPC.
items.answer: 5.8 and 4.4 units of timber (m³) per unit; opportunity cost changes, so the PPC is concave (increasing opportunity cost).
items.markingKey: First: 29/5 = 5.8; second: 22/5 = 4.4 [2]. Opportunity cost rises as more is produced because resources are not equally suited to both goods, so the curve is bowed out [2].

items.stem: A country produces only food and machinery. Explain, using a PPC, the effect of a decision to devote more resources to machinery production on present and future living standards.
items.answer: Movement along the PPC towards machinery: opportunity cost is food now (lower current consumption); more capital goods raise future productive capacity, shifting the PPC outward later; trade-off between present and future living standards.
items.markingKey: Movement along the PPC towards machinery: opportunity cost is food now (lower current consumption); more capital goods raise future productive capacity, shifting the PPC outward later; trade-off between present and future living standards.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the PPC model is too simple to be useful in analysing a real economy.
items.answer: The PPC is a simplification, but it is a powerful way of illustrating core concepts; its usefulness is conceptual rather than predictive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it shows only two goods; it assumes fixed resources and technology; it cannot show prices or the distribution of income. Arguments against: it clearly illustrates scarcity, choice and opportunity cost; it distinguishes unemployment (inside) from growth (shift); it can show trade-offs such as consumer vs capital goods. Supported judgement: The PPC is a simplification, but it is a powerful way of illustrating core concepts; its usefulness is conceptual rather than predictive. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The situation where each extra unit of one good requires giving up more and more of the other good, because resources are not equally suited to both"?
items.answer: increasing opportunity cost
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of increasing opportunity cost.

items.stem: Which of the following explains why a PPC is usually concave (bowed out) to the origin?
options: Demand for both goods falls as more is produced
Resources are not equally suited to producing both goods, so opportunity cost increases
items.answer: Resources are not equally suited to producing both goods, so opportunity cost increases
items.markingKey: C. As more of one good is produced, less suitable resources must be transferred, so more of the other good is sacrificed.

items.stem: Explain why moving along a PPC illustrates opportunity cost.
items.answer: Moving from one point to another on the curve increases output of one good only by reducing output of the other; the amount given up is the opportunity cost of the extra units.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Moving from one point to another on the curve increases output of one good only by reducing output of the other; the amount given up is the opportunity cost of the extra units. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why any point on the PPC is productively efficient.
items.answer: On the curve all resources are fully employed with the best available technology, so more of one good can only be produced by giving up some of the other – there is no waste.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: On the curve all resources are fully employed with the best available technology, so more of one good can only be produced by giving up some of the other – there is no waste. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to the Covid-19 lockdowns of 2020, explain how it illustrates a point inside the PPC.
items.answer: Many workers and factories were idle as shops, restaurants and factories closed. Resources were unemployed, so actual output fell below potential: the economy moved from a point on its PPC to a point inside it.
items.markingKey: Context (Many workers and factories were idle as shops, restaurants and factories closed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Resources were unemployed, so actual output fell below potential: the economy moved from a point on its PPC to a point inside it. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a point inside the PPC.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "If an economy is on its PPC it must be producing the best combination of goods for society." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Being on the curve means productive efficiency only; the best combination (allocative efficiency) depends on society's preferences.
items.markingKey: Being on the curve means productive efficiency only; the best combination (allocative efficiency) depends on society's preferences. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that if an economy is on its PPC it must be producing the best combination of goods for society. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Being on the curve means productive efficiency only; the best combination (allocative efficiency) depends on society's preferences.
items.markingKey: Being on the curve means productive efficiency only; the best combination (allocative efficiency) depends on society's preferences. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: Diagram: good X on the horizontal axis, good Y on the vertical axis; a concave PPC. Moving from A to B to C, each equal increase in X requires a larger fall in Y, because resources best suited to Y are increasingly used for X. Points on the curve are productively efficient; inside: unemployment; outside: unattainable.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that every economy should aim to produce at a point on its PPC.
items.answer: Producing on the PPC is desirable for productive efficiency, but the chosen point must also reflect society's preferences and sustainability.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: points inside mean wasted, unemployed resources; full use of resources maximises output. Arguments against: being on the PPC does not guarantee the right mix (allocative efficiency); full use of natural resources may be unsustainable; some unemployment (frictional) is unavoidable. Judgement: Producing on the PPC is desirable for productive efficiency, but the chosen point must also reflect society's preferences and sustainability. items.stem: Define the term "capital goods".
items.answer: Man-made goods, such as machinery and infrastructure, used to produce other goods and services
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: man-made goods, such as machinery and infrastructure, used to produce other goods and services. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims that Mass emigration of young workers shifts a country's PPC outwards because there are fewer people to feed. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Emigration reduces the quantity of labour, which reduces potential output and shifts the PPC inwards.
items.markingKey: Emigration reduces the quantity of labour, which reduces potential output and shifts the PPC inwards. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why producing more capital goods today can lead to faster economic growth in future.
items.answer: Capital goods increase the quantity of capital available for production; this raises productive capacity, shifting the PPC outward in the future, although current consumption must be sacrificed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Capital goods increase the quantity of capital available for production; this raises productive capacity, shifting the PPC outward in the future, although current consumption must be sacrificed. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Real GDP in Morocco rose from $745 billion to $774 billion over one year. Calculate the rate of economic growth.

Read the source below.

In 2023 a central bank estimated that its economy's potential output was $520 billion while actual output was $494 billion. Unemployment had risen to 7.5% from 5% a year earlier.
— Hypothetical central bank report

Using a PPC and the data, explain the position of the economy and calculate its output gap as a percentage of potential output.
items.answer: Output gap = (494 − 520)/520 × 100 = −5%: actual output is below potential, so the economy is at a point inside its PPC; rising unemployment confirms idle resources.
items.markingKey: Output gap = (494 − 520)/520 × 100 = −5%: actual output is below potential, so the economy is at a point inside its PPC; rising unemployment confirms idle resources. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Investment in capital goods is the most important cause of economic growth.
items.answer: Capital accumulation is a key cause but long-run growth depends on technology, human capital and institutions that make investment productive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: more capital raises labour productivity; infrastructure reduces costs across the economy; evidence from East Asian economies. Arguments against: human capital and technology may matter more; institutions and the rule of law are needed; investment that is wasted (unproductive projects) adds little. Supported judgement: Capital accumulation is a key cause but long-run growth depends on technology, human capital and institutions that make investment productive.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "economic growth".
items.answer: An increase in real output (real GDP) over time; long-term growth is an increase in potential output, shown by an outward shift of the PPC
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an increase in real output (real GDP) over time; long-term growth is an increase in potential output, shown by an outward shift of the PPC. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a fall in unemployment does not shift the PPC.
items.answer: Lower unemployment uses existing resources more fully, moving actual output from inside the PPC towards the curve; potential output (the curve itself) is unchanged.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Lower unemployment uses existing resources more fully, moving actual output from inside the PPC towards the curve; potential output (the curve itself) is unchanged. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why an improvement in education can lead to an outward shift of the PPC.
items.answer: Education raises human capital – the skills and productivity of labour – so more output can be produced from the same number of workers, increasing potential output.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Education raises human capital – the skills and productivity of labour – so more output can be produced from the same number of workers, increasing potential output. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Any increase in a country's GDP is shown by an outward shift of the PPC." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: If an economy moves from inside its PPC towards the curve (e.g. recovery from recession), GDP rises without the PPC shifting; only an increase in potential output shifts the curve.
items.markingKey: If an economy moves from inside its PPC towards the curve (e.g. recovery from recession), GDP rises without the PPC shifting; only an increase in potential output shifts the curve. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate the difference between actual economic growth and an increase in potential output, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: two goods on the axes; PPC1. Point A inside PPC1 moving to B on PPC1 is actual growth using idle resources (e.g. recovery). An outward shift of PPC1 to PPC2 (more resources, better technology, more human capital) is an increase in potential output; point C on PPC2 was previously unattainable.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: two goods on the axes; PPC1. Point A inside PPC1 moving to B on PPC1 is actual growth using idle resources (e.g. recovery). An outward shift of PPC1 to PPC2 (more resources, better technology, more human capital) is an increase in potential output; point C on PPC2 was previously unattainable. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Ukraine's economy contracted by about 29% in 2022 after the Russian invasion, as factories, power stations and ports were destroyed. Explain the effect on Ukraine's PPC.
items.answer: Destruction of capital and the loss of labour (displacement, mobilisation) reduced productive capacity, so the PPC shifted inwards; actual output also fell as resources were idle, moving further inside the curve.
items.markingKey: Destruction of capital and the loss of labour (displacement, mobilisation) reduced productive capacity, so the PPC shifted inwards; actual output also fell as resources were idle, moving further inside the curve.

items.stem: A government faces a choice between increasing spending on consumer goods to raise current living standards and spending on infrastructure. Using a PPC, explain the trade-off and the likely long-run outcome of each choice.
items.answer: Moving along the PPC: more consumer goods now means fewer capital goods; less capital accumulation means slower outward shifts later; choosing capital goods sacrifices current consumption but shifts the PPC further out in future, allowing more of both later.
items.markingKey: Moving along the PPC: more consumer goods now means fewer capital goods; less capital accumulation means slower outward shifts later; choosing capital goods sacrifices current consumption but shifts the PPC further out in future, allowing more of both later.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An economic system in which resources are allocated by both the price mechanism and the government, with private and public sectors"?
items.answer: mixed economy
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of mixed economy.

items.stem: Distinguish between human capital and physical capital.
items.answer: Physical capital is man-made equipment and infrastructure; human capital is the education, skills and health of workers. Both raise productivity.
items.markingKey: Physical capital is man-made equipment and infrastructure; human capital is the education, skills and health of workers. Both raise productivity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kenji writes: "In a mixed economy the government owns all the major industries." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A mixed economy has both private and public sectors; many mixed economies (e.g. Germany) have mostly private industry with government providing services and regulating.
items.markingKey: A mixed economy has both private and public sectors; many mixed economies (e.g. Germany) have mostly private industry with government providing services and regulating. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

In Venezuela, the government fixed the prices of many basic goods from 2003 and nationalised hundreds of firms. By 2016 supermarkets regularly had empty shelves and many producers had stopped production because the fixed prices were below their costs.
— Extract based on news reporting, 2016

Using the extract, explain one weakness of extensive state control of the economy.
items.answer: Fixed prices below costs removed the incentive to produce, so supply fell and shortages appeared; price signals no longer reflected scarcity, showing the information and incentive problems of planning.
items.markingKey: Fixed prices below costs removed the incentive to produce, so supply fell and shortages appeared; price signals no longer reflected scarcity, showing the information and incentive problems of planning. items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "A free market economy is the best system for allocating resources."
items.answer: Markets allocate most goods efficiently, but all successful economies are mixed because of market failure and equity concerns.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: price mechanism signals scarcity and gives incentives; consumer sovereignty and choice; competition encourages efficiency and innovation. Arguments against: market failure: public goods, externalities, merit goods; inequality of income and wealth; instability and unemployment. Supported judgement: Markets allocate most goods efficiently, but all successful economies are mixed because of market failure and equity concerns.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "free market economy"?
options: An increase in real output (real GDP) over time; long-term growth is an increase in potential output, shown by an outward shift of the PPC
An economy moving from central planning towards a market system, such as the former Soviet bloc after 1991
An economic system in which resources are allocated by the price mechanism and are mainly privately owned
Man-made goods, such as machinery and infrastructure, used to produce other goods and services
items.answer: An economic system in which resources are allocated by the price mechanism and are mainly privately owned
items.markingKey: C. "free market economy" is an economic system in which resources are allocated by the price mechanism and are mainly privately owned.

items.stem: Explain why planned economies often suffered from shortages of consumer goods.
items.answer: Planners set prices and output targets without accurate information on consumer wants; prices did not signal scarcity, managers lacked profit incentives, and resources were directed to heavy industry and defence, so queues and shortages were common (e.g. the USSR in the 1980s).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Planners set prices and output targets without accurate information on consumer wants; prices did not signal scarcity, managers lacked profit incentives, and resources were directed to heavy industry and defence, so queues and shortages were common (e.g. the USSR in the 1980s). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why almost all economies today are mixed economies.
items.answer: Markets allocate most goods efficiently, but they fail to provide public goods, under-provide merit goods and may be inequitable; governments therefore provide some goods (defence, education) and regulate markets, combining both systems.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Markets allocate most goods efficiently, but they fail to provide public goods, under-provide merit goods and may be inequitable; governments therefore provide some goods (defence, education) and regulate markets, combining both systems. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 shows the transition from a planned to a market economy.
items.answer: Russia and other former Soviet states moved rapidly from central planning to markets, privatising state firms and freeing prices. Freeing prices ended shortages but caused high inflation and a deep fall in output in the early 1990s, showing the costs of transition.
items.markingKey: Context (Russia and other former Soviet states moved rapidly from central planning to markets, privatising state firms and freeing prices.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Freeing prices ended shortages but caused high inflation and a deep fall in output in the early 1990s, showing the costs of transition. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the transition from a planned to a market economy.

items.stem: Identify the factor of production in each case: (i) a coffee plantation in Colombia; (ii) a barista; (iii) an espresso machine; (iv) the person who starts the café chain.
items.answer: (i) land; (ii) labour; (iii) capital; (iv) entrepreneurship.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "mixed economy"?
options: An economic system in which resources are allocated by both the price mechanism and the government, with private and public sectors
The maximum output an economy can produce when all resources are fully and efficiently employed, shown by the PPC itself
Man-made goods, such as machinery and infrastructure, used to produce other goods and services
A combination of goods lying outside the PPC that cannot be produced with current resources and technology
items.answer: An economic system in which resources are allocated by both the price mechanism and the government, with private and public sectors

items.stem: Distinguish between constant opportunity cost and increasing opportunity cost.
items.answer: With constant opportunity cost the PPC is a straight line because resources are equally suited to both goods; with increasing opportunity cost it is concave because resources are specialised.

items.stem: Using the Covid-19 lockdowns of 2020 as an example, explain a point inside the PPC.
items.answer: Many workers and factories were idle as shops, restaurants and factories closed. Resources were unemployed, so actual output fell below potential: the economy moved from a point on its PPC to a point inside it.
items.markingKey: Context (Many workers and factories were idle as shops, restaurants and factories closed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Resources were unemployed, so actual output fell below potential: the economy moved from a point on its PPC to a point inside it. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a point inside the PPC.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the difference between actual economic growth and an increase in potential output.
items.answer: Diagram: two goods on the axes; PPC1. Point A inside PPC1 moving to B on PPC1 is actual growth using idle resources (e.g. recovery). An outward shift of PPC1 to PPC2 (more resources, better technology, more human capital) is an increase in potential output; point C on PPC2 was previously unattainable.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: two goods on the axes; PPC1. Point A inside PPC1 moving to B on PPC1 is actual growth using idle resources (e.g. recovery). An outward shift of PPC1 to PPC2 (more resources, better technology, more human capital) is an increase in potential output; point C on PPC2 was previously unattainable. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Since 1978 China has moved from central planning towards a 'socialist market economy'. Outline two changes this involved.
items.answer: e.g. farmers allowed to sell surplus output at market prices (household responsibility system); private firms and foreign investment permitted (Special Economic Zones such as Shenzhen); prices freed for many goods; state-owned enterprises reformed.
items.markingKey: e.g. farmers allowed to sell surplus output at market prices (household responsibility system); private firms and foreign investment permitted (Special Economic Zones such as Shenzhen); prices freed for many goods; state-owned enterprises reformed.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

In 2020, India's government imposed a strict national lockdown. Official data showed GDP fell by about 24% in the April-June quarter compared with a year earlier, as millions of migrant workers lost their jobs.
— Based on data from India's National Statistical Office

Using a PPC, explain what the data suggest happened to India's economy.
items.answer: Output fell sharply while productive capacity was largely unchanged: the economy moved from a point on (or near) its PPC to a point well inside it because labour and capital were unemployed.
items.markingKey: Output fell sharply while productive capacity was largely unchanged: the economy moved from a point on (or near) its PPC to a point well inside it because labour and capital were unemployed. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: With reference to China's high investment rate since the 1990s, explain how it illustrates the link between capital goods and economic growth.
items.answer: China invested over 40% of GDP in factories, infrastructure and housing for many years. Large investment in capital goods raised productive capacity, shifting China's PPC outward and helping average growth of around 9-10% a year for three decades.
items.markingKey: Context (China invested over 40% of GDP in factories, infrastructure and housing for many years.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Large investment in capital goods raised productive capacity, shifting China's PPC outward and helping average growth of around 9-10% a year for three decades. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the link between capital goods and economic growth.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how the price mechanism answers the question 'what to produce' when consumer tastes change.
items.answer: Diagram: market for plant-based milk; demand shifts from D1 to D2 as tastes change; excess demand at the original price raises price from P1 to P2; quantity supplied rises from Q1 to Q2 along S. The higher price signals producers to allocate more resources to this good and gives them the incentive (profits) to do so; the opposite occurs in the market for dairy milk.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: market for plant-based milk; demand shifts from D1 to D2 as tastes change; excess demand at the original price raises price from P1 to P2; quantity supplied rises from Q1 to Q2 along S. The higher price signals producers to allocate more resources to this good and gives them the incentive (profits) to do so; the opposite occurs in the market for dairy milk. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Briefly describe the shift of US factories to military production during the Second World War and explain what it reveals about opportunity cost shown by a PPC.
items.answer: Car plants such as Ford's were converted to build tanks and aircraft, and civilian car production almost stopped. The economy moved along its PPC towards military goods; the opportunity cost was the civilian goods no longer produced.
items.markingKey: Context (Car plants such as Ford's were converted to build tanks and aircraft, and civilian car production almost stopped.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The economy moved along its PPC towards military goods; the opportunity cost was the civilian goods no longer produced. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to opportunity cost shown by a PPC.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that economic growth shown by an outward shift of the PPC always improves economic well-being.
items.answer: An outward shift increases potential well-being, but actual improvements depend on distribution, sustainability and what is produced.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: more goods and services can be produced; higher incomes and employment. Arguments against: growth may be unequally distributed; environmental costs and depletion of resources; the mix may be capital goods or defence rather than consumer goods. Supported judgement: An outward shift increases potential well-being, but actual improvements depend on distribution, sustainability and what is produced.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that a free market economy is the best system for allocating resources.
items.answer: Markets allocate most goods efficiently, but all successful economies are mixed because of market failure and equity concerns.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: price mechanism signals scarcity and gives incentives; consumer sovereignty and choice; competition encourages efficiency and innovation. Arguments against: market failure: public goods, externalities, merit goods; inequality of income and wealth; instability and unemployment. Judgement: Markets allocate most goods efficiently, but all successful economies are mixed because of market failure and equity concerns. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: "The PPC model is too simple to be useful in analysing a real economy." Discuss.
items.answer: The PPC is a simplification, but it is a powerful way of illustrating core concepts; its usefulness is conceptual rather than predictive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it shows only two goods; it assumes fixed resources and technology; it cannot show prices or the distribution of income. Arguments against: it clearly illustrates scarcity, choice and opportunity cost; it distinguishes unemployment (inside) from growth (shift); it can show trade-offs such as consumer vs capital goods. Supported judgement: The PPC is a simplification, but it is a powerful way of illustrating core concepts; its usefulness is conceptual rather than predictive. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "productive efficiency (on the PPC)".
items.answer: A situation where output is on the PPC, so it is impossible to produce more of one good without producing less of the other
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a situation where output is on the PPC, so it is impossible to produce more of one good without producing less of the other. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "economic growth"?
options: A situation where output is on the PPC, so it is impossible to produce more of one good without producing less of the other
An economic system in which the government owns most resources and decides what, how and for whom to produce
An increase in real output (real GDP) over time; long-term growth is an increase in potential output, shown by an outward shift of the PPC
The difference between actual and potential output, often expressed as a percentage of potential output
items.answer: An increase in real output (real GDP) over time; long-term growth is an increase in potential output, shown by an outward shift of the PPC
items.markingKey: C. "economic growth" is an increase in real output (real GDP) over time; long-term growth is an increase in potential output, shown by an outward shift of the PPC.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The factor that organises the other factors of production and takes the risks of running a business"?
items.answer: entrepreneurship
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of entrepreneurship.

items.stem: "If an economy is on its PPC it must be producing the best combination of goods for society." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Being on the curve means productive efficiency only; the best combination (allocative efficiency) depends on society's preferences.
items.markingKey: Being on the curve means productive efficiency only; the best combination (allocative efficiency) depends on society's preferences. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a movement from inside the PPC to the curve and an outward shift of the PPC.
items.answer: The first uses previously unemployed resources so actual output rises with capacity unchanged; the second increases the maximum output possible because of more or better resources or technology.
items.markingKey: The first uses previously unemployed resources so actual output rises with capacity unchanged; the second increases the maximum output possible because of more or better resources or technology. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that in a mixed economy the government owns all the major industries. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A mixed economy has both private and public sectors; many mixed economies (e.g. Germany) have mostly private industry with government providing services and regulating.
items.markingKey: A mixed economy has both private and public sectors; many mixed economies (e.g. Germany) have mostly private industry with government providing services and regulating. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a point on the PPC is not necessarily allocatively efficient.
items.answer: Every point on the curve is productively efficient, but only one combination matches the mix of goods society values most; producing too many weapons and too little food, for example, is efficient in production but not in allocation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Every point on the curve is productively efficient, but only one combination matches the mix of goods society values most; producing too many weapons and too little food, for example, is efficient in production but not in allocation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between potential growth and actual growth.
items.answer: Actual growth is a rise in real output, shown by a movement from inside towards (or along) the PPC; potential growth is an increase in productive capacity, shown by an outward shift of the PPC.
items.markingKey: Actual growth is a rise in real output, shown by a movement from inside towards (or along) the PPC; potential growth is an increase in productive capacity, shown by an outward shift of the PPC. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Money is a factor of production because firms need it to buy machines." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Money (financial capital) is not itself a factor; it is used to buy capital goods, which are the factor of production.
items.markingKey: Money (financial capital) is not itself a factor; it is used to buy capital goods, which are the factor of production. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how the discovery of large oil reserves off the coast of Guyana from 2015 affects its PPC.
items.answer: More natural resources (land) increase potential output, so the PPC shifts outward, especially along the axis of goods using oil; actual output rose rapidly as production started in 2019.
items.markingKey: More natural resources (land) increase potential output, so the PPC shifts outward, especially along the axis of goods using oil; actual output rose rapidly as production started in 2019.

items.stem: Using Singapore's Housing and Development Board (HDB) as an example, explain a mixed economy.
items.answer: Around 80% of Singapore's residents live in public housing built by the state, while the rest of the economy is highly market-oriented. Singapore combines free markets in most goods with substantial government provision of housing, showing that real economies mix both systems.
items.markingKey: Context (Around 80% of Singapore's residents live in public housing built by the state, while the rest of the economy is highly market-oriented.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Singapore combines free markets in most goods with substantial government provision of housing, showing that real economies mix both systems. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a mixed economy.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate the difference between a point inside a PPC, a point on it and a point outside it, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: concave PPC for two goods. Point inside (U): unemployed or inefficient resources, more of both goods possible. Point on (E): full employment, productive efficiency, opportunity cost in moving along the curve. Point outside (O): unattainable with current resources and technology; reachable only through economic growth (outward shift).

items.stem: "Central planning can achieve faster development than a market economy." Discuss.
items.answer: Planning may achieve rapid early industrialisation but sustained development has generally relied on markets combined with government action.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: state can mobilise savings for heavy industry quickly (USSR 1930s); can prioritise basic needs and equity. Arguments against: information and incentive problems create waste and shortages; lack of innovation and consumer choice; collapse of Soviet-style systems. Supported judgement: Planning may achieve rapid early industrialisation but sustained development has generally relied on markets combined with government action. items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that investment in capital goods is the most important cause of economic growth.
items.answer: Capital accumulation is a key cause but long-run growth depends on technology, human capital and institutions that make investment productive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: more capital raises labour productivity; infrastructure reduces costs across the economy; evidence from East Asian economies. Arguments against: human capital and technology may matter more; institutions and the rule of law are needed; investment that is wasted (unproductive projects) adds little. Judgement: Capital accumulation is a key cause but long-run growth depends on technology, human capital and institutions that make investment productive.
